paper_metadata.title: Recurrence risk after a first remote symptomatic unprovoked seizure in childhood: a prospective study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study used a consecutive recruitment strategy in a setting that serves as the sole reference for the region, ensuring high representativeness. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are clearly defined.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Torrecárdenas Hospital is the reference hospital of the province of Almería, Spain. The only electroencephalogram (EEG) laboratory and paediatric neurology unit in the province are located in this hospital.
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the geographic and clinical source of the population.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: All consecutive patients aged 14 years or less who attended our unit for a first remote symptomatic unprovoked seizure between 1 June 1994 and 1 February 2006 were included
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment from a primary reference center minimizes selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between 1 June 1994 and 1 February 2006
items.reasoning: Specific dates are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Paediatric Neurology Unit, Department of Paediatrics, Torrecárdenas Hospital, Almería, Spain.
items.reasoning: The specific hospital and department are identified.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Neonatal convulsions, patients already on antiepileptic treatment, those who had been examined previously in other centres... were excluded.
items.reasoning: Detailed criteria for both inclusion and exclusion are provided, including the 'zero time' (first seizure).

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: All consecutive patients... were included in a prospective study.
items.reasoning: The use of consecutive enrollment in a single-center reference setting suggests high participation of the eligible local population.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: General features of the cohort are shown in Table I, the aetiology in Table II, and findings on cerebral MRI in Table III.
items.reasoning: Comprehensive baseline data including age, sex, seizure type, EEG, and MRI findings are provided.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study had an exceptionally low dropout rate (only 1 patient), and the follow-up duration was sufficient to capture the majority of recurrence events.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Only one patient was lost to follow-up. In 57 patients (91%), follow-up was longer than 1 year and in 47 (75%), longer than 2 years.
items.reasoning: A loss of only 1 out of 63 patients (1.6%) is excellent for a long-term prospective study.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text does not describe specific methods used to track down the single lost patient, though the impact is negligible.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The reason for the single loss to follow-up is not stated.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Characteristics of the single lost patient are not provided separately.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Only one patient was lost to follow-up.
items.reasoning: With only one patient lost, systematic differences between completers and non-completers are statistically impossible to influence the results significantly.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Prognostic factors were measured using objective clinical standards (MRI, EEG, IQ testing) and were defined according to international guidelines.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Global developmental delay was defined as a developmental quotient <70% and intellectual disability as an intelligence quotient <70.
items.reasoning: Clear clinical thresholds and definitions are provided for the primary prognostic factors.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: an EEG and a cerebral MRI were obtained for every patient.
items.reasoning: The use of objective diagnostic imaging and neurophysiology increases reliability.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: developmental quotient <70% and intellectual disability as an intelligence quotient <70.
items.reasoning: The cut-points used for IQ/DQ are standard clinical definitions, not derived from the study data.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: an EEG and a cerebral MRI were obtained for every patient.
items.reasoning: The protocol was applied uniformly to the entire cohort.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: an EEG and a cerebral MRI were obtained for every patient.
items.reasoning: The text implies 100% completion of the baseline diagnostic workup.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no mention of missing data or imputation, though the small sample size and prospective nature suggest data was complete.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the outcome (seizure) is clearly defined, the measurement relies on parental reporting of events, which introduces potential recall or observation bias, and there is no mention of blinding.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The event under study was seizure recurrence... More than one seizure within a period of 24 hours was considered to be a single seizure
items.reasoning: The outcome and its temporal grouping are clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Parents were provided with a dose of rectal diazepam to use if a seizure lasted for more than 5 minutes.
items.reasoning: The study relies on parental observation and reporting of seizures. While standard in epilepsy research, it is less reliable than objective monitoring and lacks blinding.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were examined within a maximum interval of 15 days by one of the participant paediatric neurologists.
items.reasoning: The follow-up protocol was standardized for all participants.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study adjusted for several clinical factors, but the small sample size (n=63) limited the number of variables that could be included in the multivariable model, potentially leaving some confounding unaddressed.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Prior febrile convulsions, Family history, Age, Multiple seizure, Status epilepticus, Todd's paresis, Focal seizure, Abnormal EEG, Abnormal MRI
items.reasoning: A wide range of clinically relevant potential confounders were recorded.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: A family history of unprovoked seizures was defined as seizures occurring in first-degree relatives.
items.reasoning: Definitions for family history, status epilepticus, and developmental delay are provided.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: an EEG and a cerebral MRI were obtained for every patient.
items.reasoning: Confounders were measured using standard clinical tools.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Initial evaluation... physical and neurological examination was performed, and an EEG and a cerebral MRI were obtained for every patient.
items.reasoning: All baseline confounders were assessed during the same initial evaluation period.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No mention of missing confounder data or imputation methods.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Only two patients received antiepileptic treatment... treatment influence on the recurrence risk obtained in our study can be considered negligible.
items.reasoning: The study design minimized the confounding effect of treatment by including mostly untreated patients, but did not use matching or stratification.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Due to the small size of the sample, we decided to reduce the variables included in the multivariable analysis.
items.reasoning: While multivariable analysis was performed, the small sample size forced the exclusion of several potential confounders, which may lead to residual confounding.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are generally appropriate, but the authors admit to not validating the model due to 'computing time' and the small sample size makes the multivariable results less robust.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Recurrence risk... was calculated using Kaplan-Meier survival curves... univariable and multivariable analyses... using the Cox proportional hazards model.
items.reasoning: The analytical plan is clearly laid out.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: we selected the two variables with p<0.1... From the rest, we also selected the two variables with p<0.1... Finally, prior febrile convulsions and age <3 years were included
items.reasoning: The strategy used a mix of p-value thresholds and clinical relevance, which is acceptable but slightly data-driven.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Kaplan-Meier survival curves... Cox proportional hazards model.
items.reasoning: These are the standard and appropriate models for time-to-event (prognosis) data.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table IV: Univariable and multivariable analysis of predictors
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings for all variables tested.
